title: Conversion and caste
hook: the Ambedkarite movement today, and Buddhism as a path of dignity in India

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bamiyan, and two empty niches in a cliff. Your line: the empty niches. Day one thousand forty-three, the end of a hard week.

"Jai Bhim." In parts of India, that's how some Buddhists greet each other: victory to Bhim. Bhim is Bhimrao Ambedkar, and his portrait hangs beside the Buddha's in some homes and community halls, and on banners at gatherings. He wears a suit and glasses and holds a book. Why does a lawyer in a suit sit next to the Buddha? Today's story is about birth, about dignity, and about a choice a whole movement made.
screen: `JAI BHIM.` → `A PORTRAIT BESIDE THE BUDDHA.` → `BIRTH AND DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: An old scene fits today. A brahmin tending his sacred fire sees the Buddha on his alms round and shouts at him to stop where he is, calling him an outcast. The Buddha doesn't defend his own family. He asks whether the man even knows what makes an outcast. Then he answers: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. Deeds make a person either. That is the Vasala Sutta, and the Dhammapada says much the same. As this path told some weeks ago, B. R. Ambedkar, born into a community treated as untouchable, took refuge in the Buddha with a great crowd in Nagpur. His followers carry that choice into ordinary places. Small viharas stand in city neighborhoods and villages, his portrait beside the Buddha's. Study circles read his book, The Buddha and His Dhamma. Some families take the refuges and precepts together at weddings and naming ceremonies. Each year, on the anniversary, crowds return to the ground in Nagpur. At gatherings you'll hear his call: educate, agitate, organize. For many in the movement, dignity means schooling, work and fair treatment as well as the refuges, and some describe Buddhism as the path that gave it all a name. People of other traditions in India, Hindus among them, have also worked against caste; this isn't a contest between faiths. It's the story of people told by birth that they were less, who now greet each other with two words: Jai Bhim. So a hard week ends: Tibet in exile, Cambodia rebuilt, Saigon told with care, Mongolia and China reopening, Bamiyan's empty niches, and a path chosen for dignity. Every day, something kept.
screen: `NOT BY BIRTH, BY DEEDS.` · `VIHARAS, STUDY CIRCLES, NAGPUR.` · `EDUCATE, AGITATE, ORGANIZE.` · then, large: `A PATH OF DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone people tend to overlook, the person who cleans the building, the one who collects the trash, a neighbor others talk past, and see their face if you can. With each in-breath, notice that they have a whole life, as full as yours; with each out-breath, wish them well.
Ambedkar. The movement he began, still alive in neighborhood viharas and study circles, where worth is measured by deeds, not by birth. Today's word.
Your line: a path of dignity. Worth is measured by deeds, not by birth. That's day one thousand forty-three.

chat.says: Why do some Buddhists in India greet each other with Jai Bhim?
options: It honors Ambedkar, whose movement found dignity in the Buddha's path.
It's an old Pali greeting monks used in the Buddha's own lifetime.
It means victory to Bhima, the strong hero of the old epics.
chat.meaning: Bhim is Bhimrao Ambedkar, who took refuge in the Buddha with a great crowd in Nagpur; his followers greet each other in his name.
